title: Blog 1
content:
Overview: Diagnosing the Database Bottleneck When first learning Cloud architecture, it is easy to assume that placing an Application Load Balancer in front of an EC2 Auto Scaling Group is enough to handle any traffic spike.
I held that exact assumption until running a load test for my project. When simulated traffic jumped from a few hundred to 10,000 concurrent users:
The Auto Scaling Group scaled out right on schedule: 2 EC2 → 4 EC2 → 8 EC2 Web server CPU utilization stayed comfortably around 40–50% Yet in the browser, the homepage took 6–8 seconds to load before timing out completely Checking Amazon CloudWatch quickly revealed the real culprit: the Amazon RDS instance behind the web tier was pinned at 100% CPU.
Original Post: View on Facebook
1. How Auto Scaling EC2 Accidentally “Chokes” the Database Real-world web applications (e-commerce, news portals, forums) typically exhibit heavily skewed traffic patterns: roughly 80–90% of operations are READS (browsing product catalogs, reading articles, checking carts), while only 10–20% are WRITES.
What happens during a sudden traffic surge:
As the Auto Scaling Group launches more EC2 instances, the volume of SELECT queries hitting the single RDS instance scales proportionally Thousands of concurrent requests repeatedly fetch the exact same dataset (such as top 10 flash-sale items or leaderboards) The database continuously reads from EBS storage, burning through IOPS and CPU cycles on redundant queries and starving critical write transactions like order creation and checkout In short: the stateless web tier scales horizontally with ease, leaving a single stateful database as the sole bottleneck of the entire architecture.
2. Two Defensive Layers to Optimize Read Workloads 2.1. First Line of Defense: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) & Cache-Aside Before scaling up RDS to an expensive instance class, the first question to ask is: which data changes infrequently yet gets read the most? Instead of forcing RDS to recompute the same query 10,000 times per minute, I deployed Amazon ElastiCache for Redis inside a Private Subnet directly in front of the database using the Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) pattern:
Cache Hit: When an EC2 instance needs the featured product list, the application checks Redis first. If present in RAM, Redis serves it immediately—typically with sub-millisecond latency—without RDS ever seeing the request. Cache Miss: If the key is absent from Redis (or its TTL has expired), EC2 queries RDS, returns the result to the user, and populates Redis with an appropriate TTL (e.g., 60 seconds or 5 minutes). Cache Invalidation: Whenever data is updated in the database (such as a product price change), the application deletes or updates the corresponding Redis key so subsequent reads load fresh data rather than waiting for TTL expiration. In my lab benchmark, offloading roughly 80% of repetitive reads to Redis cut RDS CPU utilization nearly in half. Exact savings vary depending on query complexity and cache hit ratio, so always measure against your own workload.
2.2. Second Line of Defense: Amazon RDS Read Replicas For complex read queries (search filters, aggregations, reporting) that cannot be easily cached in Redis, Amazon RDS Read Replicas allow you to provision one or more read-only copies of the Primary DB via asynchronous replication.
Splitting database connections at the application layer:
Primary Endpoint: Handles all write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and reads requiring strict immediate consistency Read Replica Endpoint: Absorbs heavy analytical and general SELECT read traffic Important Note: For standard RDS for MySQL/PostgreSQL, each Read Replica exposes its own individual endpoint rather than a built-in load-balanced “reader endpoint.” When running multiple replicas, your application must distribute traffic across endpoints (or use Route 53 weighted records). A unified reader endpoint is natively provided only by Amazon Aurora (and RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters).
3. Four Real-World Pitfalls to Watch Out For While building the lab and reviewing AWS operational guides, I found that adding caching and replicas comes with four common traps:
3.1. Confusing Multi-AZ Standby with a Read Replica A common misconception is that enabling Multi-AZ gives you a second active node for read scaling. In a standard Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the synchronous standby is strictly passive for High Availability failover and cannot serve read queries. To scale reads, you must explicitly create a Read Replica. (Multi-AZ DB clusters do offer readable standbys, though that is a distinct deployment topology.)
3.2. Replication Lag Because Read Replicas replicate asynchronously, they trail slightly behind the Primary—ranging from tens of milliseconds to several seconds under peak write load. If a user submits an order (writing to Primary) and the confirmation page immediately runs a SELECT against a Read Replica, it might return “Order not found.” Always route read-after-write flows directly to the Primary endpoint.
3.3. Cache Stampede on Simultaneous TTL Expiration If thousands of cached keys expire at the exact same moment (e.g., midnight 00:00), thousands of concurrent requests will experience simultaneous cache misses and hammer RDS at once. A practical fix is adding TTL jitter (e.g., 300s + random(0..30s)) to stagger expirations. For ultra-hot keys (such as flash-sale items), combine jitter with mutex locking (allowing only one request to recompute the cache) or proactive background refresh.
3.4. Memory Eviction and ap-southeast-1 Costs Caching everything without TTLs or memory limits will fill Redis RAM and trigger key eviction, degrading your cache hit ratio. Cost-wise, in the Singapore region (ap-southeast-1), a small cache.t4g.micro node costs roughly ~$13/month (730 hours)—very affordable for student labs. However, spinning up two or three large Read Replicas and forgetting to tear them down afterward will quickly inflate your monthly AWS bill.
Conclusion Upgrading from a basic Web Scale setup to a Read-Optimized Architecture highlights three essential design principles:
Never scale up the database before checking your Read/Write ratio: Most database bottlenecks in standard web apps stem from repetitive read queries rather than write throughput limits Follow a structured optimization hierarchy: Absorb hot reads in memory (ElastiCache Redis) → offload complex reads to RDS Read Replicas → scale up the instance class only as a last resort Clean up lab resources promptly: Delete Read Replicas and ElastiCache clusters once benchmarking is done to protect your Free Tier or AWS credits (and consider connection pooling or Amazon RDS Proxy if concurrent EC2 connections become a bottleneck) References:
Amazon RDS Read Replicas Overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ReadRepl.html Amazon ElastiCache Caching Strategies (Cache-Aside): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonElastiCache/latest/dg/Strategies.html Amazon RDS Multi-AZ vs. Read Replicas: https://aws.amazon.com/rds/features/read-replicas/ Amazon ElastiCache Pricing (ap-southeast-1): https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/pricing/ Best Practices for Amazon RDS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_BestPractices.html

title: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party Hub
content:
Event Report: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party Hub Event Overview Event Name: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 – Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party Hub Date: September 29, 2026 Participation Format: Attended the in-person Watch Party in Ho Chi Minh City, following the livestreamed Keynotes and Developer Chats from the Hanoi venue alongside the AWS First Cloud Journey community. Organizers: AWS Vietnam, AWS Community Builders, and AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ). Main Topics and Insights 1. Moving from Technology Adoption to Operational Maturity A key message from the event was that Vietnam’s cloud and AI ecosystem is moving beyond Proof-of-Concept (PoC) experiments toward operating production systems reliably, securely, and at scale.
Production workloads require clearly assigned ownership, well-defined access boundaries, comprehensive observability, resilient infrastructure, and repeatable cost-management practices. These capabilities are essential for turning promising prototypes into dependable services.
2. Agentic AI and the Role of Platform Engineering Agentic AI was one of the central themes. AI systems are evolving from tools that primarily generate content into agents that can call APIs, access internal data, modify code, and initiate deployment workflows.
As these agents become more autonomous and development cycles accelerate, Platform Engineering provides important engineering guardrails. It helps standardize deployment processes, establish secure defaults, govern software supply chains, and define approval boundaries for actions performed by AI agents.
3. Workload Identity and AI Agent Security on AWS The Developer Chats session presented by Kha Van, Cloud Security Engineer and AWS Community Builder, examined an important security question: when a workload makes an AWS API request, which identity is actually being used?
The discussion highlighted the growing number of non-human identities in cloud environments, including Kubernetes Pods, CI/CD pipelines, serverless functions, and AI agents. These identities need appropriate governance just as human users do.
AWS approaches discussed included Amazon EKS Pod Identity, short-lived temporary credentials, fine-grained workload-level permissions, strict IAM trust policies, and runtime identity verification. These practices help avoid relying on overly broad permissions inherited from EC2 nodes and support the principle of least privilege.
4. AWS Infrastructure Development in Vietnam and Hybrid Architectures The event highlighted AWS infrastructure developments in Vietnam, including AWS Direct Connect in Hanoi and the Hanoi AWS Local Zone.
These options give organizations more flexibility for private connectivity, low-latency applications, and workloads with data locality requirements. They also create more choices when designing hybrid architectures that combine on-premises infrastructure and cloud services.
Architecture decisions should balance latency, resilience, compliance, security, and cost rather than focusing on only one factor.
5. Enterprise Transformation and Vietnam’s Cloud Community The TCBS Customer Story demonstrated how AI can transform software engineering when it becomes part of everyday development activities, including writing, reviewing, testing, and delivering code. The value of AI adoption should be assessed through measurable operational improvements, not simply by adding another tool to the technology stack.
The keynote also shared figures illustrating the growth of Vietnam’s cloud and AI ecosystem:
More than 157,000 individuals trained in cloud and AI. Over 54,000 members in the AWS Study Group. More than 15,000 participants in the First Cloud and AI Journey (FCJ) ecosystem. These figures reflect the increasing interest in cloud and AI knowledge among developers and technology professionals in Vietnam.
Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party Experience Although the main event took place in Hanoi, joining the Ho Chi Minh City Watch Party provided an opportunity to follow the sessions with fellow FCJ interns and mentors in person.
The local gathering made it possible to exchange ideas, discuss real-world architecture decisions, and learn from other participants while watching the livestreamed sessions. It also helped strengthen connections within the Ho Chi Minh City AWS community.
Key Takeaways and Application to My Internship 1. Adopt a Production-First Mindset A working demonstration does not automatically mean that an application is ready for production. Logging, monitoring, observability, reliability, and cost controls should be considered from the beginning of the design process.
2. Prioritize Identity-Centered Security Workloads and AI agents should not be given broad permissions simply for convenience. Temporary credentials, narrowly scoped IAM policies, and the principle of least privilege help reduce unnecessary security risks.
3. Learn and Share Through the Community Learning from experienced practitioners, mentors, and AWS Community Builders provides practical perspectives beyond technical documentation. Recording and sharing these insights can also improve my understanding of cloud architecture and engineering practices.

title: Blog 2
content:
Overview: Uncovering Hidden Private Subnet Data Transfer Charges When learning AWS network design, the first security best practice we apply is isolating application servers (EC2, ECS) inside Private Subnets so they never expose Public IPs to the Internet, while placing a NAT Gateway in a Public Subnet so private instances can still download packages and call external APIs.
I built that exact textbook architecture for a data processing project:
Backend workers on EC2 (Private Subnet) compressed logs, generated reports, and uploaded backups to Amazon S3, while reading/writing job states in Amazon DynamoDB—all within the Singapore region (ap-southeast-1) Everything ran smoothly and securely However, checking Billing & Cost Management at the end of the month brought an unwelcome surprise: beyond the fixed hourly NAT Gateway charge, NAT Gateway Data Processing added tens of dollars—even though the application barely called any external third-party APIs. The reason lies in a subtle routing detail: By default, Amazon S3 and DynamoDB reside outside your VPC and use Public IP ranges—meaning all traffic between EC2 and S3 was detouring through the NAT Gateway.
Original Post: View on Facebook
1. Why Does Internal AWS Traffic Get Billed Through a NAT Gateway? When an EC2 instance inside a Private Subnet executes aws s3 cp or writes objects via an AWS SDK:
The domain s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com resolves to a public AWS IP address EC2 evaluates the Private Route Table associated with its subnet. With no dedicated internal route for S3, packets match the catch-all default rule: 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx (NAT Gateway) Hundreds of gigabytes of backups and datasets traverse the NAT Gateway (and Internet Gateway) just to reach S3 in the exact same region NAT Gateway pricing in Singapore (ap-southeast-1):
Hourly Charge: $0.059/hour (~$43.07/month for 730 hours, even with zero traffic) Data Processing Charge: $0.059/GB for all data passing through the gateway Transferring just 500 GB/month between EC2 and S3 (system logs, media uploads, database dumps) incurs an extra $29.50/month in NAT Gateway data processing fees—for traffic that never needed to leave AWS’s regional network.
2. The Zero-Cost Solution: How VPC Gateway Endpoints Work To keep S3 and DynamoDB traffic strictly within the AWS Private Backbone without traversing a NAT Gateway or Internet Gateway, AWS provides VPC Gateway Endpoints.
2.1. Longest Prefix Match Routing Mechanics Gateway Endpoints rely on standard Longest Prefix Match route selection inside your Route Table:
You provision a VPC Gateway Endpoint (vpce-xxxx) for Amazon S3 (or DynamoDB) and associate it with your Private Route Table AWS automatically injects a route using an AWS Managed Prefix List (pl-s3-id, representing all regional S3 IP ranges) pointing directly to vpce-xxxx Packets destined for S3/DynamoDB match pl-s3-id → vpce-xxxx (more specific than 0.0.0.0/0) and travel privately over AWS’s internal network at $0/hour and $0/GB, while OS updates (apt update) and third-party API calls continue routing via 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxxx 2.2. Routing Architecture Overview Upper Path (Matched Prefix List): Same-region traffic from EC2 to S3 and DynamoDB is intercepted by the Private Route Table and routed via the VPC Gateway Endpoint ($0/GB) Lower Path (Default Route 0.0.0.0/0): Only outbound Internet requests or cross-region S3/DynamoDB calls traverse the NAT Gateway in the Public Subnet ($0.059/hour + $0.059/GB). (Note: Diagram simplified; the Internet Gateway sits between the NAT Gateway and the Internet.) 3. Four Configuration Pitfalls to Avoid 3.1. Confusing Free Gateway Endpoints with Hourly Interface Endpoints Only two AWS services support completely free Gateway Endpoints: Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB. Other services (SQS, SNS, Secrets Manager, ECR, CloudWatch, etc.) use Interface Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), which bill per AZ (~$0.01/hour/AZ plus per-GB data processing). Because S3 supports both types, accidentally selecting an Interface Endpoint will still incur hourly charges.
3.2. Forgetting to Associate the Private Route Table If you create a Gateway Endpoint without selecting your Private Subnet’s Route Table during setup, AWS will not inject the pl-s3-id → vpce-xxxx route—leaving your traffic silently flowing through the NAT Gateway.
3.3. Cross-Region Buckets Bypass Gateway Endpoints (and Trigger Double Charges) VPC Gateway Endpoints are strictly regional (e.g., EC2 in ap-southeast-1 accessing an S3 bucket in ap-southeast-1). If your bucket resides in us-east-1, its IP range falls outside Singapore’s Prefix List, forcing traffic through the NAT Gateway ($0.059/GB) plus Inter-Region Data Transfer fees.
3.4. Locking Yourself Out of Console, CLI, and SDKs with aws:SourceVpce A major security perk of Gateway Endpoints is adding a Deny rule to your S3 Bucket Policy blocking any request not originating from your vpce-xxxx (using StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpce). However, without an exemption clause, this blocks all access outside the VPC—including your own AWS Management Console, CLI, and local SDK calls (Access Denied). Always add an exclusion condition (such as ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalArn) for administrative IAM roles or users.
4. How to Verify in 30 Seconds Inspect the Route Table: Navigate to VPC → Route Tables → select your Private Route Table → Routes tab, and confirm a route with Destination pl-xxxxxxxx (com.amazonaws.ap-southeast-1.s3) pointing to Target vpce-xxxxxxxx Check NAT Gateway CloudWatch Metrics: Upload a 1–2 GB test file from EC2 to S3. On CloudWatch, the NAT Gateway’s BytesOutToDestination metric should remain flat at 0 instead of spiking Conclusion Optimizing private subnet data transfers on AWS comes down to three key takeaways:
Eliminate unnecessary NAT detours: Large S3 transfers from Private Subnets without a Gateway Endpoint incur avoidable per-GB NAT Gateway processing fees Use free VPC Gateway Endpoints: Enable Gateway Endpoints ($0) to keep same-region S3 and DynamoDB traffic on the AWS Private Backbone Double-check associations and policies: Always attach the Private Route Table, keep buckets in the same region, and include an aws:PrincipalArn exception when restricting bucket policies via aws:SourceVpce References:
Gateway VPC Endpoints: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpce-gateway.html Gateway Endpoints for Amazon S3: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html Amazon VPC & NAT Gateway Pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/ AWS PrivateLink Pricing: https://aws.amazon.com/privatelink/pricing/ AWS Managed Prefix Lists: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/managed-prefix-lists.html

title: First Cloud AI Journey: Weekly Meet Up 24/10
content:
Event Report: “First Cloud AI Journey: Weekly Meet Up 24/10” Event Information Event name: First Cloud AI Journey: Weekly Meet Up 24/10 Date: October 24, 2026 Organizers: AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ) and AWS Study Group Session Highlights 1. Building Voice AI Agents and AI-powered Recruitment Interviews Speaker: Kiet Tran – Engineer at ReAI (AWS Partner). Key topics: Introduced different approaches to building Voice AI systems, with a focus on low latency for natural conversations (a reference target of approximately 200ms). The session compared three architectures: Cascaded (ASR → LLM → TTS), Speech-to-Speech, and Full Speech-to-Speech combined with background reasoning models. Explained the call-processing flow involving SIP Servers and Media Servers (WebRTC/UDP), together with noise cancellation and Voice Activity Detection (VAD). The presented system ran on Multi-AZ GPU infrastructure, connected through AWS PrivateLink, with an overall response time of approximately 1.8 seconds. The live demo showcased an AI recruitment assistant that could call candidates and interview them on AWS topics such as EC2, S3, EKS, RDS, and VPC. Other practical topics included preparing Vietnamese text for TTS, applying Guardrails to moderate responses, and keeping operating costs at an indicative level of around VND 3,000 per call. 2. Sharing Resources Across AWS Accounts with AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) Speaker: Long – AWS Study Group. Key topics: Discussed centralized resource management in Multi-Account environments using AWS RAM. The service supports sharing more than 40 resource types, including VPC Subnets, Security Groups, and Reserved EC2 Instances, across accounts without a separate charge for the sharing operation. Explained how AWS RAM Permissions work together with IAM Policies and Service Control Policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations to govern resource access. EventBridge and CloudTrail were also mentioned as tools for monitoring related activities. Highlighted implementation considerations for Terraform and CloudFormation, particularly the need to align Availability Zone IDs across accounts to avoid unintended data-transfer costs. The Hub-and-Spoke network model was also introduced as an approach to organizing infrastructure connectivity. 3. Automated Security Testing with AWS Security Agent Speaker: Thinh – Engineer at Steel Solution. Key topics: Presented three core capabilities of AWS Security Agent. Design Review evaluates Terraform infrastructure designs to identify architectural risks early; Code & Security Review integrates with GitHub/GitLab Pull Requests and CI/CD workflows; Automated Penetration Testing simulates user behavior to identify vulnerabilities and build attack graphs in SIT/UAT environments. Discussed the Shared Responsibility Model and how security responsibilities are distributed. The session also covered using an agent or extension through a private tunnel to connect to a self-hosted GitLab server, supporting security checks while protecting internal source code. 4. Bringing AI Agents to Production with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Speaker: Nguyen Son An – Leader of the AWS Student Group at HCMUTE. Key topics: Examined challenges that arise when moving AI Agents from experimentation to production, including security, session isolation, and conversation-state management. Introduced Amazon Bedrock AgentCore through two main components: Runtime: Provides a serverless execution environment in which each session is isolated in its own MicroVM. The session discussed an EC2 Spot Instance-based infrastructure approach and cost optimization through CPU-based charging during execution. Memory: Manages information at two levels. Short-term Memory stores conversation data associated with a sessionId and supports session branching. Long-term Memory asynchronously extracts information to produce summaries and retain user preferences and long-term knowledge. 5. Improving Software Development and 24/7 Operations Automation with Kiro Speakers: Hieu Nghi – Leader of the AWS Student Group, and Khoa – Tech Lead at ACB. Key topics: Introduced Spec-Driven Development through the Plan → Design → Tasks workflow, helping teams clarify requirements and implementation steps before development. Safety measures were also discussed, such as masking secrets/passwords and requiring manual approval before potentially destructive infrastructure commands. Shared enterprise use cases for Kiro, including connecting it to Telegram to check and report AWS resource status every five minutes, as well as automating GitHub Code Reviews based on internal standards. Emphasized managing the Context Window carefully to use tokens efficiently and control costs when working with AI tools. Knowledge and Lessons Gained Architectural Thinking Learned that AI system design requires balancing response latency, language-processing quality, scalability, and operating costs. Gained a better understanding of Multi-Account infrastructure, resource sharing, and selecting suitable connectivity models for different system requirements. Security Throughout the Development Lifecycle Recognized the importance of introducing security checks early in the development lifecycle, from Infrastructure as Code design to Pull Request reviews. Understood that security should be maintained throughout development and operations rather than being treated as a final-stage activity. Emerging AWS AI Technologies and Tools Gained further insight into operating AI Agents in production with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, particularly session and memory management. Explored how Kiro can support specification-driven development, code reviews, and automation of operational tasks. Applying the Knowledge to My Internship Project The discussion of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore helped me better understand the considerations involved in integrating AI capabilities into the Smart Kitchen project. The sessions on security, monitoring, and cost optimization also provided useful ideas for reviewing and improving the way AWS services are deployed in the project. The event reinforced the importance of evaluating solutions based on actual requirements, complexity, and cost instead of adopting technologies simply because they are trending. Event Experience The event provided an opportunity to learn about several technologies and practices used in real-world environments, ranging from Voice AI and multi-account resource management to automated security testing and production AI Agents. The examples and demonstrations helped me better understand how AWS services and tools can work together to address practical business and engineering challenges.
Beyond the technical content, I learned to evaluate solutions from multiple perspectives, including architecture, security, performance, operability, and cost. These insights are valuable for my ongoing learning and for improving my internship project.

title: Proposal

SMART KITCHEN SMART KITCHEN PLATFORM A proposal to develop a platform that supports food discovery, home cooking, and finding nearby ingredient suppliers.
Information Details Project source code repository https://github.com/veexto/AWS-Final-Project-Cooking/tree/main Deployed website https://d18x1ou8x7botm.cloudfront.net/ AWS Region Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 Date November 2026 1. Background and Motivation 1.1. Project Background In modern life, choosing meals, finding cooking recipes, and preparing ingredients are common needs. However, information about dishes, cooking instructions, and ingredient suppliers is often scattered across multiple platforms. Users may spend time finding meals that match the ingredients they have, their budget, and their shopping options.
Smart Kitchen is a web platform that helps users discover dishes, explore home-cooking recipes, and find ingredient suppliers based on their current location or a manually entered address. The project uses AWS services to deploy the frontend, process requests, store data, connect to location search services, and integrate AI capabilities through Amazon Bedrock.
1.2. Motivation and Objectives Simplify food discovery and help users choose recipes that match their needs. Provide ingredient information and cooking instructions to support home cooking. Help users find nearby ingredient suppliers based on their current location or a provided address. Build an AWS-hosted web application with an architecture that can be maintained and scaled. Integrate Amazon Bedrock to add generative AI request-processing capabilities to the application. 1.3. Expected Outcomes A website accessible through its AWS deployment URL. Users can browse, search, and filter the recipe data available in the system. Users can view dish ingredients and cooking instructions. The system can receive location search requests and return results from Amazon Location Service. The system can send requests to Amazon Bedrock and receive responses from the integrated AI model. The user interface, server-side processing, database, and AI services are connected through AWS services. 2. Solution Architecture 2.1. Architecture Overview Smart Kitchen uses a serverless web architecture on AWS. Frontend files and static assets are stored in Amazon S3, while Amazon CloudFront is configured as the content delivery layer in front of S3. When users access the website through the CloudFront domain, CloudFront receives the requests, serves content from the S3 origin, and can cache content at edge locations to improve page-loading performance. Business requests generated by user interactions are sent directly from the frontend to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS, then forwarded to AWS Lambda for processing. Lambda retrieves recipe data from Amazon DynamoDB, calls Amazon Location Service when location searches are required, or calls Amazon Bedrock when AI functionality is needed.
Amazon Bedrock is integrated into the server-side processing flow. AWS Lambda acts as an intermediary that receives requests, sends prompts to the AI model, and processes the responses before returning results to the user interface. This approach keeps service credentials and access permissions on the server side instead of exposing them in frontend source code.
2.2. AWS Architecture Diagram 2.3. AWS Services and Their Roles AWS Service Role in the Project Amazon S3 Stores the website’s frontend files and static assets. Amazon CloudFront Acts as the content delivery network (CDN) in front of Amazon S3, receives website access requests, serves frontend files from S3, and helps accelerate content delivery through caching at edge locations. Users access the website through the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. Amazon API Gateway Provides API endpoints for communication between the user interface and server-side processing. AWS Lambda Receives and processes business logic, retrieves data, and orchestrates calls to AWS services. Amazon DynamoDB Stores and retrieves cooking recipe data. Amazon Location Service Supports location/store searches based on a user’s location or entered address. Amazon Bedrock Provides access to generative AI models; the project integrates Amazon Nova Micro to process AI requests from the application. 2.4. Main Application Workflows Website access: Users open the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. CloudFront receives the request and serves frontend files from S3; content can be cached at edge locations to reduce loading time when requested again. Recipe discovery: The user interface sends a request to API Gateway; Lambda processes the request and retrieves recipe data from DynamoDB before returning the results. Location search: Users provide their GPS location or enter an address; Lambda calls Amazon Location Service and returns the results to the user interface. AI request processing: The user interface sends a request to API Gateway; Lambda receives and validates the input, then calls Amazon Bedrock with the Amazon Nova Micro model. Lambda receives the model response, processes the result, and returns it to the user interface. 2.5. Scalability and Reliability Using AWS-managed and serverless services reduces the need to manage servers and allows individual components to scale according to demand. Amazon S3 stores the frontend, while CloudFront distributes content from S3 to users and supports edge caching. API Gateway and Lambda handle the application’s business requests, and DynamoDB provides the data storage layer. Amazon Location Service and Amazon Bedrock are invoked when the application needs location search or AI processing capabilities.
Monitoring, alerting, backup, and performance optimization mechanisms will be considered according to operational needs and budget. For Amazon Bedrock, request volume, service quotas, and response times must be monitored to minimize any negative impact on the user experience.
3. Security Design 3.1. Identity and Access Management Apply the principle of least privilege and grant each component only the permissions it requires. Use IAM roles for Lambda when accessing DynamoDB, Amazon Location Service, and Amazon Bedrock. Grant only the permissions required to invoke Bedrock models, such as the InvokeModel action for the model being used. Do not place access keys, secret keys, or credentials in frontend source code or public repositories. Separate AWS resource administration permissions from the application’s execution permissions. 3.2. Data and API Protection Prefer HTTPS for connections between users and the website/API; users access the website through the CloudFront domain over HTTPS. Validate and verify input data before processing. Do not expose sensitive information, credentials, or internal implementation details in API responses. Configure CORS, authentication, and request rate limits according to the application’s actual requirements. Control the content sent to Amazon Bedrock and avoid sending unnecessary personal or sensitive data. Process and validate AI model responses before returning results to the user interface. 3.3. Monitoring and Logging Amazon CloudWatch can be used to monitor logs, errors, and metrics from Lambda and related AWS components. For the Bedrock integration workflow, model invocation errors, response times, and quota usage should be monitored. Log retention periods, alert configurations, and monitoring levels will be adjusted according to operational needs and budget. Credentials and sensitive user data must not be written to logs.
4. Project Scope and Deliverables 4.1. Project Scope A. Food and Recipe Discovery Display a list of cooking recipes. Support searching and discovering dishes based on the designed criteria. Display ingredient information and cooking instructions. Provide recipe data for users to reference when cooking at home. B. Finding Nearby Ingredient Suppliers Allow users to provide their current location by granting GPS permission or manually entering an address. Send location search requests to the server-side processing layer. Use Amazon Location Service to find relevant places and return the results to the user interface. C. AI Integration with Amazon Bedrock Integrate Amazon Bedrock into server-side processing to handle AI requests from the application. Use the Amazon Nova Micro model through the server-side processing workflow. Receive requests from the user interface, send them to the AI model, and return responses to the user interface. Handle errors that occur during model invocation and service responses. 4.2. Future Development Scope Expand personalized recommendations based on users’ ingredients, budgets, preferences, and needs. Improve the integration of recipe data and AI responses to help users plan meals. Expand food-service discovery capabilities and connections with restaurants/businesses. 4.3. Out of Scope Full online payment processing. Inventory management and real-time stock synchronization. Delivery services or real-time order tracking. Comprehensive management of restaurant business operations. Large-scale data analytics. 4.4. Project Deliverables The Smart Kitchen website deployed on AWS. A user interface stored in Amazon S3 and distributed through Amazon CloudFront. A backend/API using API Gateway and AWS Lambda. A recipe database in Amazon DynamoDB. A location search feature integrated with Amazon Location Service. An AI feature integrated with Amazon Bedrock using the Amazon Nova Micro model. Project proposal documentation and an overall architecture diagram. 5. Implementation Roadmap The project is divided into major phases. The schedule may be adjusted according to actual progress and team resources.
Phase Main Activities Deliverables Phase 1: Planning Identify the problem, objectives, requirements, and project scope. Project requirements and plan. Phase 2: Application Development Build the user interface, server-side processing, and core features. User interface and server-side processing. Phase 3: AWS Infrastructure and Data Set up S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB. Deployed and connected application components. Phase 4: External Service and AI Integration Integrate Amazon Location Service and Amazon Bedrock; configure the required access permissions, connect the Amazon Nova Micro model to server-side processing, and test the response workflow. Location search and AI features integrated into the application. Phase 5: Documentation and Handover Complete project documentation, architecture, cost estimation, and Workshop materials. Project documentation package. Start and end dates will be added according to the actual implementation schedule; weekly activity records are presented in the Worklog section.
6. AWS Cost Estimation 6.1. Estimation Basis and Assumptions Costs are estimated for approximately 100–500 active users per month, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 region. This represents a small-to-medium operating scenario using a serverless architecture and includes only the services currently present in the Smart Kitchen architecture.
The assumptions used for the estimate are:
Approximately 100–500 active users per month. Approximately 20,000–100,000 requests to API Gateway per month. Approximately 1,000–5,000 location search requests through Amazon Location Service per month. Amazon Bedrock usage is estimated at 50 calls per user per month, equivalent to 5,000 calls for 100 users and 25,000 calls for 500 users. Each call uses an average of 1,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. Frontend files, images, and recipe data require relatively little storage; no continuously running EC2 instances are used. CloudFront traffic is estimated at 20 GB and 20,000 HTTPS requests per month for the 100-user scenario, and 100 GB and 100,000 HTTPS requests per month for the 500-user scenario. The table records the AWS Pricing Calculator results before considering any eligible offers or free usage allowances. 6.2. Estimated Costs by User Scale The following table summarizes the estimated costs from the AWS Pricing Calculator for scenarios with 100 and 500 active users per month. All prices are calculated for the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 region, in USD/month.
AWS Service 100 users/month (USD) 500 users/month (USD) Amazon S3 0.04 0.18 Amazon CloudFront 2.42 12.12 Amazon API Gateway (REST API) 0.09 0.43 AWS Lambda 0.01 0.05 Amazon DynamoDB 0.01 0.05 Amazon Bedrock (Nova Micro) 0.71 3.53 Amazon Location Service 0.55 2.75 Amazon CloudWatch 0.07 0.37 Estimated total/month 3.90 19.48 According to the current AWS Pricing Calculator results, the estimated cost is USD 3.90/month for 100 users and USD 19.48/month for 500 users. These are estimates based on assumed usage, not actual invoices.
Calculation details:
Amazon S3: 1 GB/5 GB of storage; 500/2,500 Tier 1 requests; 20,000/100,000 Tier 2 requests. Amazon CloudFront: 20 GB/100 GB of data transfer out to the Internet; 20,000/100,000 HTTPS requests. Amazon API Gateway: 20,000/100,000 REST API requests. AWS Lambda: 625/3,125 GB-seconds, assuming 128 MB of memory and an average execution time of 1 second. Amazon DynamoDB: 10,000/50,000 read request units and 10,000/50,000 write request units. Amazon Bedrock: 5,000/25,000 units of 1,000 input tokens and 2,500/12,500 units of 1,000 output tokens; assuming 50 calls per user per month, with 1,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens per call. Amazon Location Service: 100/500 Geocode requests and 1,000/5,000 SearchNearby requests. Amazon CloudWatch: 0.1/0.5 GB of log ingestion and 0.1/0.5 GB-Mo of log storage. The CloudFront costs in the table reflect the amounts currently displayed by the Calculator for the entered usage levels. When determining the actual budget, the account’s pricing plan, Free Tier/offer eligibility, and applicable free allowances must be checked. These amounts should not be assumed to be free until eligibility has been verified.
6.3. Factors That May Affect Costs Amazon Location Service: Number of store/place searches and the type of data requested in each request. Amazon Bedrock: Number of Nova Micro model calls and the input/output token volume of each request. Amazon CloudFront: Amount of distributed data and number of HTTPS requests; the Calculator results should be checked against the AWS account’s pricing plan and eligible free allowances. API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB: Number of requests, execution time, data volume, and query patterns. Amazon S3 and CloudWatch: Storage volume, number of read/write operations, and log retention period. 6.4. Cost Control and Optimization Measures Review AWS Billing regularly and configure budget alerts. Avoid repeated Amazon Location Service calls when users have not changed their location or search criteria. Control the number of Amazon Bedrock calls, prompt length, and response token count. Optimize CloudFront caching for static frontend files. Optimize DynamoDB queries and Lambda execution time. Periodically compare estimates with actual costs and adjust the budget based on system usage. This estimate is intended to illustrate the potential operating costs when the application serves 100–500 users per month. Once actual operating data is available, the assumptions in the AWS Pricing Calculator should be updated to produce a more accurate estimate for the system’s usage.
7. Project Management, Risks, and Conclusion 7.1. Project Team and Responsibilities Member Role Responsibilities Huỳnh Minh Hiệp Frontend Developer & UI/UX Designer Design and develop the website interface; build food search and filtering features, display recipes, and connect the frontend to the backend. Nguyễn Nguyên Vũ Backend Developer Develop the backend using AWS Lambda and API Gateway; build APIs, implement search and recipe recommendation logic, and integrate Amazon Bedrock to support the AI chatbot. Nguyễn Mạnh Dũng AWS Cloud Engineer & Database Developer Configure and deploy AWS services such as S3, CloudFront, DynamoDB, Amazon Location Service, and CloudWatch; manage recipe data and support system testing and operations. 7.2. Risk Assessment and Mitigation Risk Impact Mitigation AWS service quotas Some services or models may encounter quota or access limitations. Monitor quotas, verify access permissions, and adjust usage accordingly. API errors The user interface may not receive data from server-side processing. Enable logging, handle exceptions, and check API status. Database performance Queries may become slow as data volume or traffic increases. Optimize data design and query patterns. Location result accuracy Location results may be incomplete or inaccurate. Allow manual address entry and validate returned results. AI response quality AI-generated responses may be inaccurate or unsuitable for a request. Validate input data, process responses, and provide appropriate notices to users. AI availability and service limits AI requests may fail when the service is unavailable or usage limits are reached. Handle errors, monitor quotas, and notify users when a response cannot be generated. Unexpected AWS costs Costs may increase when traffic or service usage exceeds estimates. Monitor Billing, control requests/tokens, and configure budget alerts. 7.3. Conclusion Smart Kitchen aims to provide a platform that helps users discover dishes, explore cooking recipes, and find ingredient suppliers. The use of Amazon S3, CloudFront, API Gateway, AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and Amazon Location Service provides the foundation for deploying the application’s core features on AWS. In addition, Amazon Bedrock with the Amazon Nova Micro model has been integrated into server-side processing to provide generative AI request-processing capabilities for the application.
This proposal defines the project’s background, objectives, architecture, scope, security requirements, implementation plan, costs, and key risks. Detailed evidence of integration, source code, and test results is presented in the Workshop/Deployment Evidence section.

title: Configure the AWS IAM Role
content:
The Lambda function needs permissions to read data from DynamoDB, invoke the conversational model in Amazon Bedrock, and query places through Amazon Location Service (geo-places v2).
Procedure Go to IAM → Roles → Create role. Select AWS service → Lambda → choose Next. Name the role RecipesLambdaRole and choose Create role. Open RecipesLambdaRole, select Add permissions → Create inline policy, name it RecipesLambdaPolicy, and paste the following JSON: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadMealRecipesTable", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "dynamodb:Scan", "dynamodb:Query", "dynamodb:GetItem" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:*:table/RecipesTable" }, { "Sid": "SearchNearbyStoresV2", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "geo-places:SearchText" ], "Resource": "*" }, { "Sid": "InvokeBedrockChefAI", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "bedrock:InvokeModel" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:*:inference-profile/apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0", "arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/amazon.nova-micro-v1:0" ] }, { "Sid": "WriteCloudWatchLogs", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:CreateLogGroup", "logs:CreateLogStream", "logs:PutLogEvents" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:ap-southeast-1:*:log-group:/aws/lambda/RecipeSearchFunction:*" } ] } Open RecipesLambdaRole again, select Add permissions → Create inline policy, name it AmazonLocationGeoPlacesAccess, and paste the following JSON: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "geo-places:SearchNearby", "geo-places:SearchText", "geo-places:Geocode", "geo-places:ReverseGeocode" ], "Resource": "*" } ] }

title: Blog 3
content:
Overview: Achieving Data Reproducibility with Amazon S3 Versioning and SHA-256 When building data engineering pipelines or ML training workflows on AWS, most of us initially set up a deceptively clean storage pattern:
A daily ETL Ingestion job overwrites the latest dataset at a single static S3 path, such as s3://data-lake-bucket/clean/dataset.csv Downstream Lambda functions or EC2 workers read that fixed key to generate reports or train models Everything runs smoothly until you need to audit historical numbers: you check out last week’s exact Git commit and re-run the pipeline against s3://data-lake-bucket/clean/dataset.csv, only to get completely different outputs from the submitted report. At that point, you have no way to tell whether a recent code refactor introduced a bug or whether yesterday’s ETL job silently overwrote dataset.csv. Without pinning input data versions, debugging and compliance audits turn into pure guesswork.
Original Post: View on Facebook
1. Why You Should Not Rely on S3 ETag for File Integrity When looking for a quick way to verify whether an S3 object has changed, many developers (myself included) reach for the ETag field returned by S3 APIs. However, ETag is a classic trap:
Only valid for Single-Part Uploads with SSE-S3: S3 only sets ETag to the raw MD5 digest of the file when uploaded in a single operation (single-part upload) using default SSE-S3 encryption Breaks under Multipart Upload & SSE-KMS: Once a file exceeds the SDK’s multipart threshold (Multipart Upload) or the bucket uses SSE-KMS encryption, ETag is no longer the MD5 of the entire object (for multipart uploads, it becomes the MD5 of the concatenated part MD5s followed by the part count, e.g., "...-5") Comparing a locally computed file hash against S3’s ETag will falsely flag intact files as corrupted. Instead of relying on ETag, the reliable approach is pairing SHA-256 checksums (via S3’s native ChecksumAlgorithm='SHA256' or application-side hashing) with S3 Versioning.
2. Combining S3 Versioning with a DynamoDB SHA-256 Manifest To reproduce the exact input dataset for any historical pipeline run with 100% certainty, combine three building blocks:
2.1. Enable S3 Versioning on the Data Bucket Every time the ETL job overwrites clean/dataset.csv, S3 preserves the previous object and assigns the new upload a unique VersionId (e.g., v1, v2). Older revisions become Noncurrent Versions and remain completely immutable—nobody can alter the bytes stored under an existing VersionId.
2.2. Record a Run Manifest in Amazon DynamoDB Whenever a pipeline starts a new execution (Run ID), it persists a Manifest record capturing the Bucket, Key, exact VersionId consumed, and the object’s SHA-256 digest.
2.3. Read by Pinned VersionId and Verify SHA-256 Before Processing When re-running an earlier job for auditing or backtesting, the pipeline ignores the unversioned key (which always resolves to the latest v2) and instead queries the DynamoDB Manifest, calls GetObject with VersionId=v1, computes the SHA-256 hash of the downloaded byte stream, and compares it against the stored manifest. Only upon an exact match does processing proceed; any mismatch or missing version triggers an immediate Fail Fast abort rather than producing silent data corruption.
3. Pipeline Data Reproducibility Architecture ETL Ingestion: Continuously overwrites the dataset key on Amazon S3. With Versioning enabled, v1 remains preserved alongside v2 Step 1 (Manifest DB): The Pipeline Runner writes or reads the pinned object metadata (VersionId + SHA-256 hash) in Amazon DynamoDB Step 2 (GetObjectVersion): The Pipeline Runner retrieves the exact pinned object version (v1) rather than accidentally pulling the latest v2 Step 3 (Integrity Check): Compares the live SHA-256 hash against the manifest—proceeding only on a match and failing fast on any discrepancy Automated Cleanup: An S3 Lifecycle Rule periodically expires aged noncurrent versions (NoncurrentVersionExpiration) to keep storage costs bounded 4. Four Implementation Pitfalls to Watch Out For 4.1. Granting s3:GetObject While Forgetting s3:GetObjectVersion In IAM policies, s3:GetObject only authorizes reading the current version of an object. The moment your pipeline passes a VersionId parameter to reproduce historical data, AWS denies the request with AccessDenied unless the IAM Role also includes s3:GetObjectVersion.
4.2. Silent S3 Bill Growth from Unmanaged Noncurrent Versions In Singapore (ap-southeast-1), every noncurrent version on S3 Standard is billed at full storage rates ($0.025/GB/month for the first 50 TB). Overwriting a 10 GB dataset daily for 30 days means paying for 300 GB ($7.50/month instead of $0.25/month), even though the default S3 Console view (with Show versions toggled off) displays only a single file. Always configure an S3 Lifecycle Rule to transition older versions to cheaper storage tiers (NoncurrentVersionTransition) or expire them after a retention window (NoncurrentVersionExpiration).
4.3. Standard DeleteObject Calls Do Not Free Storage On a versioned bucket, calling DeleteObject without specifying a VersionId does not delete any underlying bytes—it merely inserts a Delete Marker as the latest version. All prior versions remain stored and billed monthly until explicitly deleted by their VersionId.
4.4. Trusting ETag Across Multipart Uploads or SSE-KMS As highlighted in Section 1, always store and validate SHA-256 checksums (using S3’s built-in ChecksumSHA256 support or streaming hash calculation) rather than treating ETag as a cryptographic integrity signature.
5. How to Verify in 30 Seconds Verify on the S3 Console: Open your bucket → toggle “Show versions” at the top of the object list → confirm each overwrite creates a distinct Version ID row without erasing prior revisions Test the Fail Fast Safeguard: Manually alter a single character in the SHA-256 string stored in your DynamoDB Manifest and re-trigger the pipeline → verify that the job immediately halts and raises an integrity validation error Conclusion Ensuring reproducible inputs for ETL and AI/ML pipelines on AWS comes down to three core practices:
Never rely solely on unversioned S3 paths when you need to reproduce historical pipeline runs Pin inputs with S3 Versioning + SHA-256 Manifests (instead of ETag) to guarantee byte-for-byte reproducibility Pair IAM permissions with Lifecycle rules: Include s3:GetObjectVersion in your execution role and configure S3 Lifecycle Rules to prevent noncurrent versions from inflating storage bills References:
Using Versioning in S3 Buckets: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Versioning.html Checking Object Integrity in Amazon S3 (SHA-256): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity.html Managing Noncurrent Versions with S3 Lifecycle: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-configuration-examples.html Amazon S3 Pricing (ap-southeast-1): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/

title: Blogs AWS
content:
Blog 1 - Web Auto Scaling Works Great, So Why Do 10,000 Users Still See Endless Loading Spinners? This article dissects database-tier bottlenecks that emerge when a horizontally scaled web tier (Auto Scaling Group) faces 10,000 concurrent users. It walks through a two-tier read optimization strategy combining Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) with a Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) pattern and Amazon RDS Read Replicas to offload heavy read queries, while highlighting four common operational pitfalls: confusing Multi-AZ Standby instances with Read Replicas, asynchronous replication lag, Cache Stampede expiration spikes, and cost management in the Singapore (ap-southeast-1) region.
Blog 2 - S3 and EC2 Are in the Same Region—Why Does My NAT Gateway Bill Keep Climbing Every Month? This article uncovers the hidden intra-region data processing charges incurred when compute workloads inside a Private Subnet communicate with Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB through a default 0.0.0.0/0 route traversing a NAT Gateway. It explains how VPC Gateway Endpoints leverage Longest Prefix Match routing to keep traffic within the AWS Private Backbone at $0/GB, alongside four critical configuration traps: distinguishing Gateway from Interface Endpoints, associating Private Route Tables, same-region constraints, and adding aws:PrincipalArn exclusions when locking down S3 Bucket Policies with aws:SourceVpce.
Blog 3 - Re-Running Last Week’s Pipeline Produced Completely Different Numbers: Was It a Code Change or an Overwritten S3 File? This article tackles data reproducibility for ETL pipelines and AI/ML training workflows on AWS when upstream S3 objects are continuously overwritten. Rather than relying on S3 ETag values—which break down under Multipart Uploads or SSE-KMS encryption—it outlines an architecture pairing Amazon S3 Versioning (pinning immutable VersionId references) with an Amazon DynamoDB Manifest storing SHA-256 checksums for Fail-Fast integrity validation, plus practical notes on s3:GetObjectVersion IAM permissions and S3 Lifecycle Rules for cleaning up noncurrent versions.

title: First Cloud AI Journey: Weekly Meet Up 14/11
content:
Event Overview Event Name: First Cloud AI Journey: Weekly Meet Up 14/11 Date: November 14, 2026 Speakers: Nguyễn Lâm Anh, Trần Phương Huyền, Phúc Khang, Huỳnh An Khương, Nguyễn Quốc Bảo (AWS First Cloud Journey – FCJ Members) Organizers: AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ) & AWS Study Group Session Overview On November 14, 2026, the AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ) community continued its technical learning series with an AWS Cloud Mastery session dedicated to the development of Amazon Bedrock Agents. The main objective was to explore how AI solutions can evolve from early prototypes into secure and production-ready applications.
Hosted at the AWS Vietnam office in Ho Chi Minh City, the session gathered students and aspiring technology professionals to examine the architecture behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Instead of focusing only on building basic chatbot demonstrations, the speakers discussed the engineering requirements for deploying AI agents in real business environments, with particular attention to security, reliability, and scalability.
Key Technical Highlights 1. Understanding the Transition from AI Prototypes to Production Systems The session began with the topic “From Prototype to Production: Secure, Reliable, Scalable Enterprise AI on the Cloud.” It emphasized that creating a functional AI chatbot is only the first step; operating an enterprise-level AI agent requires a much more comprehensive engineering approach.
Three major challenges were discussed:
Performance and Cost Optimization: Ensuring that AI agents respond efficiently while controlling model inference expenses and infrastructure costs, especially when handling increasing numbers of requests. System Integration and Access Control: Allowing agents to communicate with business applications and external services while enforcing clear permission boundaries and preventing unauthorized operations. Monitoring and Quality Evaluation: Observing the agent’s reasoning process and tool usage, as well as assessing whether its generated responses and executed actions meet the expected requirements. 2. Designing Scalable Solutions with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The speakers explored how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can support enterprise environments involving hundreds of agents, thousands of tools, hundreds of MCP servers, and more than 100,000 tenants.
Several important components and architectural concepts were introduced:
Authentication and Authorization for Inbound and Outbound Requests:
The session explained a reusable Universal 5-Step Skeleton for managing secure interactions through Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and AgentCore Identity. Incoming requests must be authenticated using mechanisms such as JWT or IAM credentials before agents are permitted to access external tools or MCP servers. This approach establishes controlled communication between users, AI agents, and connected services. Context and Conversation Management with AgentCore Memory:
Short-term Memory: Maintains conversation messages and session information synchronously, allowing the agent to retain the context of an ongoing interaction. Long-term Memory: Uses an automatic memory extraction process to analyze previous interactions asynchronously and organize useful information into different categories: Semantic: Knowledge and meaningful information extracted from interactions. User Preferences: User-specific habits and preferences. Summarization: Shortened summaries of previous conversations. Episodic: Records of previous tasks and experiences that can help guide future actions. Production-Level AWS Infrastructure:
The discussion also covered deploying applications across multiple Availability Zones (Multi-AZ) to improve availability and fault tolerance. Important infrastructure elements included separating public and private subnets, implementing load balancing, establishing an agent orchestration layer, and integrating observability throughout the system. These architectural practices help create a more resilient foundation for AI applications operating at scale. Interactive Atmosphere & Community Networking Technical Discussions and Audience Q&A: The session encouraged active participation from students and technology enthusiasts in Ho Chi Minh City. Questions covered practical topics such as restricting AI agent permissions when connecting to production backends, managing operational expenses, and preparing for career opportunities in Cloud and AI. Knowledge Review Through an Interactive Quiz: An interactive quiz was organized toward the end of the session to reinforce the technical concepts presented. Participants reviewed topics including Gateway authorization, AgentCore short-term and long-term memory, and Multi-AZ infrastructure deployment. Upcoming Community Activities: Before the session concluded, the organizers introduced AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026, an upcoming major event aimed at creating additional opportunities for students to learn, exchange ideas, and connect with members of the AWS community. Key Takeaways Building Beyond a Functional Prototype: I learned that developing an enterprise-ready AI agent involves more than implementing conversational features. Security controls through Gateway and Identity, structured long-term memory, and continuous behavioral monitoring should be considered from the beginning.
Understanding the Complete Architecture: The session helped me gain a broader perspective on combining Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Multi-AZ VPC infrastructure. This combination provides important foundations for building highly available and scalable AI systems capable of supporting large numbers of agents, tools, and tasks.
Continuous Learning Through the AWS Community: Attending specialized technical sessions at the AWS office provided valuable opportunities to explore emerging AWS services, understand practical implementation approaches, and gain architectural knowledge from experienced speakers and community members.

title: Week 3 Worklog

Explore EC2 compute fundamentals and the relationship between instances, storage, and network security.
