title: Deploy the AWS Lambda Backend
content:
1. Create the Lambda Function Go to AWS Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch. Configure the basic settings: Function name: RecipeSearchFunction Runtime: Python 3.12 Execution role: Select Use an existing role → RecipesLambdaRole. Go to Configuration → General configuration → Edit and increase the Timeout to 15 seconds. Go to Configuration → Environment variables and add these two environment variables: DYNAMODB_TABLE: RecipesTable BEDROCK_MODEL_ID: apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0 2. Architecture and Functionality Breakdown of lambda_function.py The lambda_function.py source code is organized into six main functional blocks. Together, they handle the complete request flow: receiving HTTP requests, validating input, connecting to three core AWS services (DynamoDB, Amazon Location Service, and Amazon Bedrock), and returning JSON responses to the frontend.
2.1. Configuration and AWS SDK Client Initialization import base64 import json import logging import math import os import random import unicodedata import urllib.error import urllib.request from decimal import Decimal from urllib.parse import parse_qs, quote import boto3 from botocore.exceptions import ClientError logger = logging.getLogger() logger.setLevel(logging.INFO) REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1") BEDROCK_REGION = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_REGION", REGION).strip() TABLE_NAME = os.environ.get("DYNAMODB_TABLE", "RecipesTable").strip() BEDROCK_MODEL_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_MODEL_ID", "apac.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0").strip() BEDROCK_API_KEY = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_API_KEY", "").strip() MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 200 MAX_KEYWORDS = 10 dynamodb = boto3.resource("dynamodb", region_name=REGION) table = dynamodb.Table(TABLE_NAME) geo_places_client = boto3.client("geo-places", region_name=REGION) bedrock_client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=BEDROCK_REGION) CORS_HEADERS = { "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*", "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "Content-Type,Authorization", "Access-Control-Allow-Methods": "GET,POST,OPTIONS", "Content-Type": "application/json; charset=utf-8", } Main functions: Reads environment variables (AWS_REGION, BEDROCK_REGION, DYNAMODB_TABLE, BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, BEDROCK_API_KEY) to separate configuration from source code, making settings easier to change without modifying the code. Initializes AWS connections (boto3.resource / boto3.client) at global scope: table (DynamoDB), geo_places_client (Location Service Places v2), and bedrock_client (Bedrock Runtime). Defining them outside lambda_handler allows connections to be reused across warm starts, reducing response latency. Configures CORS_HEADERS so browsers accessing the application through the CloudFront domain can call the API (GET, POST, OPTIONS) without being blocked by browser security policies. 2.2. Utility Functions, Normalization, and Input Validation def json_default(value): if isinstance(value, Decimal): return int(value) if value % 1 == 0 else float(value) raise TypeError(f"Unsupported JSON value: {type(value).__name__}") def response(status_code, body): return { "statusCode": status_code, "headers": CORS_HEADERS, "body": json.dumps(body, ensure_ascii=False, default=json_default), } json_default() & response(): Converts DynamoDB Decimal values to JSON-compatible int/float values and packages HTTP responses with status codes (200, 400, 500) and CORS headers. def normalize(value): text = str(value or "").strip().lower() text = text.replace("đ", "d") text = unicodedata.normalize("NFD", text) return "".join(ch for ch in text if unicodedata.category(ch) != "Mn") normalize(): Normalizes Vietnamese text into lowercase, accent-free strings (converting đ -> d and decomposing Unicode with NFD). This improves ingredient and mood-keyword matching even when users omit diacritics. def csv_values(value, field_name): if not value: return [] if len(value) > MAX_INPUT_LENGTH: raise ValueError(f"Tham số {field_name} vượt quá {MAX_INPUT_LENGTH} ký tự.") values = [part.strip() for part in value.split(",") if part.strip()] if any(len(part) > 60 for part in values): raise ValueError(f"Mỗi giá trị trong {field_name} tối đa 60 ký tự.") return [v for v in values[:MAX_KEYWORDS] if not any(c in v for c in "<>{}$`\\;")] csv_values(): Checks the maximum input length (MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 200), limits input to 10 keywords (MAX_KEYWORDS = 10), and removes potentially unsafe special characters (<>{}$\\;`) to help prevent injection. def query_params(event): params = event.get("queryStringParameters") or {} if params: return params raw = event.get("rawQueryString", "") return {k: v[0] for k, v in parse_qs(raw).items() if v} def parse_json_body(event): body = event.get("body") or "{}" if event.get("isBase64Encoded"): body = base64.b64decode(body).decode("utf-8") try: return json.loads(body) except (TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError): raise ValueError("Dữ liệu gửi lên không phải JSON hợp lệ.") query_params() & parse_json_body(): Standardizes parameter parsing for both API Gateway REST API v1 and HTTP API v2 event formats, including Base64 decoding when required. 2.3. Recipe Retrieval and Filtering (Amazon DynamoDB) def get_all_recipes(): items = [] kwargs = {} while True: result = table.scan(**kwargs) items.extend(result.get("Items", [])) last_key = result.get("LastEvaluatedKey") if not last_key: break kwargs = {"ExclusiveStartKey": last_key} items.sort(key=lambda x: str(x.get("RecipeID", ""))) logger.info("Loaded %s recipes from %s", len(items), TABLE_NAME) return items get_all_recipes(): Scans all records in the RecipesTable table, automatically handling pagination through LastEvaluatedKey when the dataset is large, and sorts the results by RecipeID. def matches(recipe, filters): ingredients = recipe.get("Ingredients") or [] allergens = recipe.get("Allergens") or [] nutrition = recipe.get("Nutrition") or {} if filters["ingredients"] and not has_any(ingredients, filters["ingredients"]): return False if filters["health"] and not has_tag(recipe, "HealthTags", filters["health"]): return False if filters["need"] and not ( has_tag(recipe, "HealthTags", filters["need"]) or has_tag(recipe, "DietTags", filters["need"]) ): return False if filters["mood"] and not has_tag(recipe, "MoodTags", filters["mood"]): return False if filters["allergies"] and ( has_any(ingredients, filters["allergies"]) or has_any(allergens, filters["allergies"]) ): return False if filters["avoid"] and has_any(ingredients, filters["avoid"]): return False numeric_rules = ( ("maxTime", "CookingTimeMinutes"), ("maxBudget", "EstimatedCostVND"), ) for param, field in numeric_rules: if filters[param] is not None: try: value = float(recipe.get(field)) except (TypeError, ValueError): return False if value > filters[param]: return False for param, field in (("maxSodium", "SodiumMg"), ("maxCarbs", "CarbsG")): if filters[param] is not None: try: value = float(nutrition[field]) except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError): return False if value > filters[param]: return False return True matches(): Applies multiple filters to each recipe: available ingredients (ingredients), allergies (allergies), ingredients to avoid (avoid), dietary and health requirements (health, need), mood (mood), and numeric limits (maxTime, maxBudget, maxSodium, maxCarbs). def ingredient_score(recipe, keywords): ingredients = [normalize(v) for v in (recipe.get("Ingredients") or [])] return sum(1 for term in keywords if any(normalize(term) in ing for ing in ingredients)) def handle_recipe_search(params, context): filters = { "ingredients": csv_values(params.get("ingredients", ""), "ingredients"), "allergies": csv_values(params.get("allergies", ""), "allergies"), "avoid": csv_values(params.get("avoid", ""), "avoid"), "health": (params.get("health") or "").strip(), "need": (params.get("need") or "").strip(), "mood": (params.get("mood") or "").strip(), "maxTime": None, "maxBudget": None, "maxSodium": None, "maxCarbs": None, } allowed_tags = { "health": {"low_sodium", "controlled_carb", "low_saturated_fat", "light", "high_protein"}, "need": {"high_protein", "vegetarian", "vegan", "low_calorie"}, "mood": {"comforting", "fresh", "energizing", "light"}, } for key, allowed in allowed_tags.items(): if filters[key] and filters[key] not in allowed: return response(400, {"error": f"Giá trị bộ lọc {key} không hợp lệ."}) numeric_limits = { "maxTime": (600, 0), "maxBudget": (10000000, 0), "maxSodium": (100000, 0), "maxCarbs": (1000, 0), } for key, (upper, lower) in numeric_limits.items(): raw = params.get(key) if raw not in (None, ""): try: value = float(raw) except (TypeError, ValueError): return response(400, {"error": f"Tham số {key} phải là số."}) if value < lower or value > upper: return response(400, {"error": f"Tham số {key} nằm ngoài giới hạn cho phép."}) filters[key] = value logger.info( "RequestId=%s filters=%s random=%s", getattr(context, "aws_request_id", "local"), filters, params.get("random") == "true", ) recipes = get_all_recipes() matched = [item for item in recipes if matches(item, filters)] matched.sort(key=lambda item: ingredient_score(item, filters["ingredients"]), reverse=True) if params.get("random", "false").lower() == "true": random.shuffle(matched) matched = matched[:6] return response(200, { "recipes": matched, "count": len(matched), "filters": filters, "source": "dynamodb", }) ingredient_score() & handle_recipe_search(): Scores ingredient matches so recipes matching more of the supplied ingredients appear higher in the results returned by GET /search. 2.4. Geolocation and Nearby Ingredient Stores (Amazon Location Service) def haversine_meters(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2): r = 6371000 phi1, phi2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2) dphi = math.radians(lat2 - lat1) dlambda = math.radians(lon2 - lon1) a = math.sin(dphi / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(phi1) * math.cos(phi2) * math.sin(dlambda / 2) ** 2 return int(2 * r * math.atan2(math.sqrt(a), math.sqrt(1 - a))) def handle_nearby_stores(params): ingredients = (params.get("ingredients") or "thực phẩm tươi").strip() if len(ingredients) > MAX_INPUT_LENGTH: raise ValueError(f"Tham số ingredients vượt quá {MAX_INPUT_LENGTH} ký tự.") tier = (params.get("tier") or "mid").strip().lower() if tier not in ("low", "mid", "high"): tier = "mid" address = (params.get("address") or "").strip() if len(address) > 200: raise ValueError("Địa chỉ tìm kiếm tối đa 200 ký tự.") try: lat = float(params.get("lat", 10.7769)) lng = float(params.get("lng", 106.7009)) except (TypeError, ValueError): lat, lng = 10.7769, 106.7009 tier_config = { "low": "Ngân sách tiết kiệm (< 35.000đ): Ưu tiên chợ truyền thống và cửa hàng tạp hóa gần bạn.", "mid": "Ngân sách vừa phải (35.000đ – 70.000đ): Ưu tiên Bách Hóa Xanh, WinMart+, Co.op Food, Satrafood.", "high": "Ngân sách thoải mái (> 70.000đ): Ưu tiên siêu thị lớn (Co.opmart, WinMart, Lotte Mart, GO!, Tops Market).", } advice = tier_config[tier] resolved_address = "" if address: query_addr = ( address if ("viet nam" in normalize(address) or "vietnam" in normalize(address)) else f"{address}, Việt Nam" ) geo_items = [] try: geo_res = geo_places_client.geocode( QueryText=query_addr, BiasPosition=[lng, lat], MaxResults=1, Language="vi", Filter={"IncludeCountries": ["VNM"]}, ) geo_items = geo_res.get("ResultItems", []) except Exception: logger.exception("Geocode failed for address=%r, trying search_text", query_addr) if not geo_items: try: st_res = geo_places_client.search_text( QueryText=query_addr, BiasPosition=[lng, lat], MaxResults=1, Language="vi", Filter={"IncludeCountries": ["VNM"]}, ) geo_items = st_res.get("ResultItems", []) except Exception: logger.exception("SearchText address lookup failed for address=%r", query_addr) if not geo_items or not geo_items[0].get("Position"): return response(200, { "source": "amazon-location-geo-places", "advice": f"Không tìm thấy tọa độ cho địa chỉ '{address}'. Hãy thử ghi rõ tên đường, phường/quận, thành phố.", "selectedTier": tier, "origin": {"lat": lat, "lng": lng}, "stores": [], }) pos = geo_items[0]["Position"] lng, lat = float(pos[0]), float(pos[1]) resolved_address = (geo_items[0].get("Address") or {}).get("Label") or geo_items[0].get("Title") or address logger.info("Resolved manual address=%r -> (%s, %s) [%s]", address, lat, lng, resolved_address) excluded_name_terms = ( "famima", "familymart", "family mart", "circle k", "gs25", "7-eleven", "ministop", "cheers", "shop&go", "shop and go", "fumart", "nha hang", "quan an", "cafe", "coffee", "tra sua", "spa", "hotel", "dien may", "me va be", "baby", "kids", "pet", "thuoc", "pharmacy", ) excluded_category_terms = ( "restaurant", "cafe", "coffee", "fast food", "food court", "bar", "pub", "gas station", "pet store", "clothing", "hotel", "lodging", ) queries_by_tier = { "low": ["chợ", "cửa hàng tạp hóa", "bách hóa"], "mid": ["Bách Hóa Xanh", "WinMart+", "Co.op Food", "Satrafood", "cửa hàng thực phẩm"], "high": ["Co.opmart", "WinMart", "Lotte Mart", "GO!", "Tops Market", "Emart", "Kingfoodmart", "siêu thị"], } try: stores_by_key = {} for search_term in queries_by_tier[tier]: try: text_result = geo_places_client.search_text( QueryText=search_term, BiasPosition=[lng, lat], MaxResults=15, Filter={"IncludeCountries": ["VNM"]}, Language="vi", ) except Exception: logger.exception("SearchText failed for query=%r", search_term) continue for item in text_result.get("ResultItems", []): title = (item.get("Title") or "").strip() if not title: continue title_norm = normalize(title) if any(term in title_norm for term in excluded_name_terms): continue categories = item.get("Categories") or [] category_names = [ normalize(category.get("LocalizedName") or category.get("Name") or "") for category in categories ] if any( excluded in category for category in category_names for excluded in excluded_category_terms ): continue pos = item.get("Position") if not pos or len(pos) < 2: continue store_lat, store_lng = float(pos[1]), float(pos[0]) dist_m = haversine_meters(lat, lng, store_lat, store_lng) if dist_m > 10000: continue addr_label = (item.get("Address") or {}).get("Label") or "Gần vị trí đã chọn" chain_names = [ chain.get("Name", "") for chain in (item.get("BusinessChains") or []) if chain.get("Name") ] category_label = ", ".join( category.get("LocalizedName") or category.get("Name", "") for category in categories if category.get("LocalizedName") or category.get("Name") ) dedup_key = (title_norm, round(store_lat, 4), round(store_lng, 4)) if dedup_key in stores_by_key: continue stores_by_key[dedup_key] = { "name": title, "address": addr_label, "distanceMeters": dist_m, "lat": store_lat, "lng": store_lng, "category": category_label, "businessChains": chain_names, "budgetGroup": tier, } selected_stores = sorted(stores_by_key.values(), key=lambda x: x["distanceMeters"]) return response(200, { "source": "amazon-location-geo-places", "advice": advice, "resolvedAddress": resolved_address, "selectedTier": tier, "origin": {"lat": lat, "lng": lng}, "searchRadiusMeters": 10000, "stores": selected_stores[:20], }) except Exception: logger.exception("Amazon Location nearby stores failed") return response(200, { "source": "fallback", "advice": advice, "resolvedAddress": resolved_address, "origin": {"lat": lat, "lng": lng}, "stores": [], }) Determine the search center (lat, lng): If the user enters a manual address (address), the function calls geo_places_client.geocode() (with search_text() as a fallback) to convert the Vietnamese address into coordinates. If the address is empty, it uses the GPS coordinates provided by the browser. Search for retailers based on the budget tier (tier): Maps the budget tiers (low, mid, high) to relevant store keyword groups (markets/grocery stores, Bách Hóa Xanh/WinMart+/Co.op Food, or Co.opmart/Lotte Mart/GO!), then calls geo_places_client.search_text() with BiasPosition centered on the user’s coordinates. Filter irrelevant results and calculate distances (haversine_meters): Excludes places that do not sell groceries (such as cafés, restaurants, spas, and gas stations), removes duplicate locations, calculates straight-line distances in meters within a 10 km radius, and sorts results from nearest to farthest for GET /nearby-stores. 2.5. AI Chef Chatbot for Mood-Based Suggestions (Amazon Bedrock) def find_recipes_by_mood_weather(msg, items): norm_msg = normalize(msg) # 1. Ưu tiên cao nhất: Khớp trực tiếp tên món ăn (chính xác hoặc gần đúng) exact_name_matches = [] partial_name_matches = [] for r in items: r_name = normalize(r.get("Name", "")) if not r_name: continue if r_name == norm_msg or r_name in norm_msg: exact_name_matches.append(r) elif len(norm_msg) >= 4 and norm_msg in r_name: partial_name_matches.append(r) if exact_name_matches: # Ưu tiên tên món dài hơn (khớp chi tiết hơn) lên đầu, không shuffle exact_name_matches.sort(key=lambda r: len(normalize(r.get("Name", ""))), reverse=True) return exact_name_matches, True if partial_name_matches: partial_name_matches.sort(key=lambda r: len(normalize(r.get("Name", "")))) return partial_name_matches, True # 2. Ưu tiên thứ hai: Khớp theo nguyên liệu xuất hiện trong câu nhắn (xếp theo số nguyên liệu khớp) ing_scored = [] for r in items: ings = [normalize(ing) for ing in (r.get("Ingredients") or []) if normalize(ing)] matched_ings = [ing for ing in ings if ing in norm_msg] if matched_ings: # Ưu tiên món khớp nhiều nguyên liệu hơn ing_scored.append((len(matched_ings), r)) if ing_scored: ing_scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) top_count = ing_scored[0][0] top_ing_recipes = [r for cnt, r in ing_scored if cnt == top_count] random.shuffle(top_ing_recipes) rest_ing_recipes = [r for cnt, r in ing_scored if cnt < top_count] return top_ing_recipes + rest_ing_recipes, False # 3. Ưu tiên thứ ba: Khớp theo tâm trạng / thời tiết / chế độ ăn target_moods = [] target_cats = [] if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["mua", "lanh", "se lanh", "buon", "stress", "ap luc", "am bung", "co don"]): target_moods.append("comforting") target_cats.extend(["soup", "main"]) if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["nong", "oi buc", "nang", "ngan", "nhe bung", "giam can", "thanh dam", "mat"]): target_moods.extend(["fresh", "light"]) target_cats.extend(["salad", "side", "soup"]) if any(k in norm_msg for k in ["met", "duoi", "ue oai", "can nang luong", "doi", "tap gym", "vui"]): target_moods.append("energizing") target_cats.append("main") scored = [] for r in items: score = 0 r_moods = r.get("MoodTags") or [] if any(m in r_moods for m in target_moods): score += 2 if r.get("Category") in target_cats: score += 1 if ("chay" in norm_msg or "thanh dam" in norm_msg) and "vegetarian" in (r.get("DietTags") or []): score += 3 if score > 0: scored.append((score, r)) scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) if not scored: return [], False top_score = scored[0][0] top_group = [r for score, r in scored if score >= max(1, top_score - 1)] random.shuffle(top_group) rest_group = [r for score, r in scored if score < max(1, top_score - 1)] return top_group + rest_group, False find_recipes_by_mood_weather(): Analyzes the meaning of the user’s message (for example, cold rainy weather, sadness, stress, hot weather, or fatigue) and maps it to MoodTags (comforting, fresh, light, energizing) and suitable food categories. It also excludes recipes suggested in previous turns (excludeIds) to avoid repetition. def handle_chat(event): payload = parse_json_body(event) user_message = str(payload.get("message") or "").strip() if not user_message: raise ValueError("Vui lòng nhập tâm trạng, thời tiết hoặc câu hỏi của bạn.") if len(user_message) > 500: raise ValueError("Câu hỏi tối đa 500 ký tự.") items = get_all_recipes() shuffled_items = list(items) random.shuffle(shuffled_items) exclude_ids = set(payload.get("excludeIds") or []) matched_recipes, is_explicit_dish = find_recipes_by_mood_weather(user_message, items) if is_explicit_dish: candidate_recipes = matched_recipes else: fresh_matches = [r for r in matched_recipes if r.get("RecipeID") not in exclude_ids] candidate_recipes = fresh_matches if fresh_matches else matched_recipes suggested_id = candidate_recipes[0].get("RecipeID") if candidate_recipes else None suggested_name = candidate_recipes[0].get("Name") if candidate_recipes else None menu_context = "\n".join([ f"- [{r.get('RecipeID')}] {r.get('Name')}: loại {r.get('Category')}, " f"tâm trạng phù hợp: {', '.join(r.get('MoodTags') or [])}, " f"chi phí ~{r.get('EstimatedCostVND')}đ, nấu {r.get('TotalTimeMinutes') or r.get('CookingTimeMinutes', 20)} phút, " f"nguyên liệu: {', '.join(r.get('Ingredients') or [])}" for r in shuffled_items ]) avoid_note = "" if exclude_ids: avoid_names = [r.get("Name") for r in items if r.get("RecipeID") in exclude_ids] if avoid_names: avoid_note = f"\n4. KHÔNG gợi ý lại các món người dùng vừa xem ở lượt trước: {', '.join(avoid_names)}. Hãy chọn món khác trong danh sách." primary_hint = ( f"2. Gợi ý món **{suggested_name}** (hoặc 1–2 món phù hợp khác TỪ DANH SÁCH BÊN DƯỚI, ghi rõ tên món chính xác, chi phí và thời gian nấu), giải thích ngắn gọn vì sao món đó hợp với tâm trạng/thời tiết hiện tại.\n" if suggested_name else "2. Gợi ý 1–2 món phù hợp nhất TỪ DANH SÁCH BÊN DƯỚI (ghi rõ tên món chính xác, chi phí và thời gian nấu), giải thích ngắn gọn vì sao món đó hợp với tâm trạng/thời tiết hiện tại.\n" ) system_prompt = ( "Bạn là Đầu Bếp AI Tâm Lý trên website hướng dẫn dạy nấu ăn Việt Nam. title: Chat with Dr. Werner
content:
Event Overview Event Name: Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Exploring the Future of Cloud and AI in Vietnam Guest Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels (Vice President & Chief Technology Officer at Amazon) Date: October 2, 2026 Organizers: AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ), AWS Heroes, and AWS Community Builders Vietnam Major Insights from the Fireside Chat 1. Lessons from Amazon’s Distributed Systems Journey and the Evolution of DynamoDB Addressing Database Limitations at Scale: Dr. Werner reflected on challenges Amazon encountered more than two decades ago, when traditional relational database systems struggled to handle the growing traffic during major holiday shopping periods. By examining real customer access patterns together with his intern Swami, who is now VP of AI at AWS, the engineering team found that approximately 70% of database requests were straightforward Key-Value lookups. This discovery became an important foundation for Dynamo, which eventually influenced the development of Amazon DynamoDB.
Building Reliability into Engineering Culture:
Prioritizing Tail Latency: Rather than depending on average response times, Amazon focused on measuring and improving performance at the 99.9th percentile (p99.9) to better understand the experience of users facing the slowest responses. Practicing Game Days: Teams deliberately simulated major infrastructure failures, including disconnecting an entire data center or Availability Zone. These exercises helped identify single points of failure, automate recovery procedures, and establish reliable data reconciliation processes when infrastructure became available again. Changing the Cloud Consumption Model: Amazon moved away from traditional IT arrangements that required large upfront commitments over several years and embraced a pay-as-you-go approach, giving customers greater flexibility and control over their spending. 2. Developing the “Renaissance Developer” Mindset in the Age of AI Dr. Werner described five important characteristics that engineers should develop to remain effective as technology and AI continue to evolve:
Curiosity and Continuous Learning: Programming languages, development environments, and tools never remain static. Engineers have moved from technologies such as C and Java toward Rust, while development workflows have evolved from traditional IDEs to tools like Kiro and Cursor. Staying curious and continuously learning is therefore essential.
Systems Thinking: Developers should understand how different services and components work together across an entire distributed system. Looking beyond individual tasks or isolated components helps engineers recognize dependencies and make better architectural decisions.
Effective Communication: Communication is often an underestimated engineering skill. Developers need to understand the real business needs behind customer requests and explain technical decisions in terms of their benefits, costs, and limitations. For example, a checkout system may require 99.99% availability, while a recommendation service may operate with 99.9%. Engineers should make these decisions based on actual requirements instead of automatically using GenAI for every problem.
Ownership and Accountability: AI-powered coding assistants can improve productivity, but they do not replace engineering responsibility. Developers remain accountable for the quality of their code, potential security weaknesses, and compliance requirements before software is released into production.
Broad Technical Knowledge with Deep Expertise: The ideal engineer combines strong knowledge in a particular specialization with practical understanding of related areas such as UI development, business logic, security, and formal verification. This T-shaped or polymath approach supports collaboration in small and flexible Two-Pizza Teams, typically consisting of around 10–12 members.
3. Combining AI-Assisted Prototyping with Amazon’s Working Backwards Approach Accelerating Development Without Sacrificing Discipline: Amazon’s Working Backwards methodology begins by defining the customer experience through internal PR/FAQ documents before implementation starts. AI-assisted prototyping can make this process faster by helping teams explore ideas and build early demonstrations. However, development speed should not come at the expense of quality. Engineers still need to evaluate the risk of each change and apply an appropriate level of code review instead of accepting AI-generated code without verification.
Using AI to Enhance Human Capabilities: Dr. Werner emphasized that technology should ultimately create value for people. AI should be treated as a tool that strengthens human capabilities rather than replacing them. Qualities such as sound judgment, creativity, empathy, and professional pride remain important in designing and maintaining reliable systems, including the infrastructure and services that users may never directly see.
Key Takeaways and Personal Reflections Select Technology Based on Actual Requirements: The discussion reminded me that adopting GenAI simply because it is popular is not always the right decision. Engineers should first evaluate workload requirements and consider the trade-offs between cost, latency, and operational reliability before choosing a solution.
Take Responsibility for AI-Assisted Development: When using AI coding assistants in projects, developers must carefully review generated code, test its behavior, identify potential security issues, and understand what they are deploying. AI can support implementation, but responsibility for the final product remains with the engineer.
Improve Communication and Think Beyond Individual Components: I gained a better understanding of why technical decisions should be connected to business objectives. Developing systems thinking and communicating architectural trade-offs clearly are essential skills. I also recognize the value of sharing technical knowledge and experiences with other members of the AWS First Cloud Journey community.

title: Workshop
content:
Bếp Thông Minh (Smart Kitchen) – AWS Workshop Overview This workshop documents the implementation and deployment of Bếp Thông Minh (Smart Kitchen), a recipe recommendation application built with AWS managed services. The application helps users discover recipes based on available ingredients, budget, cooking time, dietary preferences, mood, and weather. It also provides nearby ingredient-store lookup.
The solution separates the static frontend from the serverless backend. Amazon S3 stores the frontend files, while Amazon CloudFront delivers the website over HTTPS. Amazon API Gateway exposes the application endpoints and invokes AWS Lambda. The Lambda function retrieves recipe data from Amazon DynamoDB and integrates with Amazon Location Service for address geocoding and nearby place searches. Amazon Bedrock is integrated for conversational recipe suggestions, with a fallback response path when model invocation is unavailable.
AWS Services AWS Service Purpose Amazon S3 Hosts the static frontend files Amazon CloudFront Delivers the frontend over HTTPS Amazon API Gateway Exposes the application HTTP routes AWS Lambda Handles recipe search, nearby-store lookup, and chatbot requests Amazon DynamoDB Stores recipe records Amazon Location Service Geocodes manually entered addresses and searches for nearby stores Amazon Bedrock Supports AI-based recipe suggestions Amazon CloudWatch Stores Lambda execution logs Workshop Contents Overview and Prerequisites Create the DynamoDB Database Configure the AWS IAM Role Deploy the AWS Lambda Backend Configure Amazon API Gateway Deploy the Frontend to S3 and CloudFront Application Testing Clean Up Resources

title: Deploy the Frontend to S3 and CloudFront
content:
Technical note: Modern web browsers block the GPS geolocation API (navigator.geolocation) when a website runs over http://. Therefore, deploying Amazon CloudFront to provide HTTPS is required.
1. Configure Amazon S3 . Create an S3 bucket named recipe-suggestion-website and clear Block all public access. . Add a bucket policy that allows public read access:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PublicReadGetObject", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::recipe-suggestion-website/*" } ] } .Enable static website hosting with template.html as the index document, then upload template.html to the bucket root.
2. Configure Amazon CloudFront Go to CloudFront → Create distribution and set the origin domain to your S3 bucket (leave Origin path empty).
. Under Viewer protocol policy, select Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
. Under Web Application Firewall (WAF), select Do not enable security protections to minimize costs.
. Under Settings, set Default root object to template.html, then choose Create distribution.
. When the status changes to Deployed, access the application through https://<id>.cloudfront.net.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Participating in the Workforce Bootcamp - First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program gave me an opportunity to better understand how cloud knowledge can be applied to a practical product. Through learning, hands-on practice, and project development, I gained a broader perspective on building applications on AWS and identified several areas that could be improved to make the experience more effective for future participants.
The following comments are based on my personal experience and perspective.
1. Positive Aspects of the Program Learning Content Combined with Hands-on Practice Learning about AWS services and applying them to a project made the concepts easier to understand than studying theory alone. While developing Smart Kitchen, I had the opportunity to see how the frontend, APIs, backend, database, and supporting services connect and work together within one system.
Opportunities for Independent Learning and Experimentation The practical activities encouraged me to read documentation, review configurations, and find ways to address issues that arose during implementation. This was valuable because it helped me develop independent research habits instead of relying entirely on pre-defined instructions.
A Practical Final Project Building a specific product gave the learning process a clear objective. Tasks such as frontend deployment, API development, data storage, location search, and exploring AI integration allowed me to connect several concepts from the program within one problem.
2. Challenges I Encountered A broad range of learning topics: AWS offers many services, each with its own configuration, limitations, and pricing model. For beginners, it can sometimes be difficult to determine where to start and how deeply each topic should be studied. Time-consuming troubleshooting: An issue may be caused by IAM permissions, API configuration, input data, or service quotas. Without experience in reading logs and tracing application workflows, identifying the root cause can take considerable time. Estimating costs during early development: Some services charge based on requests, data transfer, usage duration, or consumed resources. Learners need guidance on how to monitor costs from the beginning of a project. Keeping project documentation synchronized: When configurations or architecture change, guides, diagrams, and deployment information also need to be reviewed so that the documentation remains consistent with the actual system. 3. Suggestions for Improving the Program Provide a progressive hands-on learning path: Organize the content from foundational concepts to complete deployment, with clear learning outcomes and required knowledge for each stage. This would help beginners follow their progress and identify knowledge gaps. Add verification checklists after each lab: In addition to configuration instructions, provide validation steps such as checking service status, testing API calls, reviewing logs, and confirming stored data. Checklists would help learners understand what successful completion looks like. Include more realistic troubleshooting scenarios: Introduce common situations such as missing IAM permissions, API errors, incorrect CORS settings, mismatched data, or service quota limits. Each scenario could explain how to narrow down the cause rather than simply providing a sample configuration. Integrate cost management and security from the beginning: Show learners how to configure budget alerts, review Billing, clean up resources after practice, and apply the IAM least-privilege principle. Schedule progress and architecture reviews: Short review sessions at key milestones could help learners identify design issues early and avoid extensive changes near the end of a project. Standardize documentation and evidence requirements: Provide clear checklists for the proposal, workshop, architecture diagram, demo video, and final report. This would help learners prepare in advance and ensure that submitted materials accurately reflect the implementation status. 4. Expectations for Future Programs I hope future programs will continue combining foundational knowledge with project-based practice. In addition to introducing services, more examples of design decisions, common errors, service limitations, and cost evaluation would help learners understand how to approach real-world cloud problems.
I would also welcome more opportunities for technical discussions and project presentations at different stages. Receiving feedback while a project is still in development would help learners make timely adjustments and improve their ability to explain their technical decisions.
5. Acknowledgements I appreciate the opportunity to participate in FCAJ and gain hands-on experience with AWS services. The program helped me recognize both the knowledge I have acquired and the skills I still need to improve. I would like to thank the organizing team, mentors, and everyone who shared their knowledge and provided support, motivating me to continue learning and developing in the cloud computing field.
